drills.name: Jab
drills.desc: The lead-hand straight — boxing's range-finder and most-thrown punch. Snap comes from a small push-step off the rear foot and a relaxed arm that fires and returns on the same line. It measures distance, blinds the opponent and opens every combination.
mistakes: Telegraphing by dipping the shoulder or pulling the hand back first.
Leaving the jab extended instead of snapping it straight back to the guard.
Reaching with the arm alone — no step, no weight behind it.

drills.name: Cross
drills.desc: The rear-hand power straight. Push off the rear foot, rotate hip and shoulder together, and land with the knuckles turned over.
mistakes: Rear heel stays planted — hip can’t rotate through.
Dropping the lead hand while punching.

drills.name: Lead hook
drills.desc: A short, horizontal punch thrown with the elbow up and the arm locked at roughly 90 degrees. Power comes from pivoting the lead foot and whipping the hips — the arm just carries what the body generates. Deadly at close range and the classic counter over a lazy jab.
mistakes: Swinging wide like a haymaker instead of keeping the elbow bent and tight.
Lead foot doesn’t pivot — the punch becomes all arm.
Dropping the rear hand and eating the counter hook.

drills.name: Rear uppercut
drills.desc: A vertical punch driven upward through the opponent's centre line, usually at close range. Dip the legs slightly, then extend hips and knees while rotating — the fist rides the leg drive, it doesn't scoop with the arm. Best thrown when the opponent leans forward or covers up.
mistakes: Winding up by dropping the fist to the hip — telegraphs the shot.
Punching with the arm instead of extending through the legs.
Throwing it at long range where it has no leverage.

drills.name: Body hook
drills.desc: A hook driven into the ribs or liver with the knuckles turned and the body bent to the same level as the target. Change levels with the legs, then rotate through — a clean liver shot ends fights that head punches can't. Get down to the body; never just drop the arm.
mistakes: Bending at the waist instead of the knees to change level.
Dropping the punching hand on the way in and exposing the chin.
Punching flat with a vertical fist — turn the knuckles into the ribs.

drills.name: 1-2-3 combinations
drills.desc: Linking punches so each shot loads the next: the cross's rotation coils the lead hook, the hook re-coils the cross. Rhythm and weight transfer matter more than the speed of any single punch. Finish every combination back in stance behind the guard.
mistakes: Throwing three separate punches instead of one connected sequence.
Squaring up mid-combination and losing the stance.
Holding the breath — exhale sharply on every shot.

drills.name: High guard & block
drills.desc: The fundamental cover: gloves glued to the temples, elbows tucked over the ribs, chin down. Absorb shots on the gloves and forearms while the eyes stay open, looking for the counter. Endurance in the shoulders is what keeps the guard up in round three.
mistakes: Elbows flaring out and leaving the ribs open to body shots.
Closing the eyes or turning the head away under fire.
Hiding behind the guard passively instead of countering off the block.

drills.name: Parry & return
drills.desc: Deflecting a straight punch with a small tap of the rear glove — inches of redirection, never a big swat. The parry keeps the hand close to the face and immediately opens the line for the counter jab or cross. Timing beats strength here.
mistakes: Slapping wide at the punch and dragging the hand away from the face.
Parrying without answering — every parry should buy a counter.
Reaching for feints and getting pulled out of position.

drills.name: Slip & roll
drills.desc: Rhythmic defensive movement: slipping outside punches and rolling under hooks. Legs and obliques do the work; eyes stay on the target.
mistakes: Bending at the waist instead of the knees.
Taking eyes off the opponent during the roll.

drills.name: Shoulder roll
drills.desc: The lead shoulder rides high to deflect the right hand while the rear glove guards the chin — the style Mayweather made famous. Punches roll off a subtle turn of the torso, leaving the rear hand free to counter instantly. Demands sharp reading of the opponent and constant micro-adjustments from the legs.
mistakes: Rolling flat-footed — without the legs the shell gets walked down.
Letting the rear hand drift away from the chin.
Using the shell against volume punchers without adjusting — it leaks against flurries.

drills.name: Stance & step drill
drills.desc: Moving in every direction while the stance never breaks: the foot nearest the direction of travel steps first, the other drags to restore width. Weight stays on the balls of the feet, knees soft, head over hips. Everything in boxing sits on top of this.
mistakes: Crossing the feet — one trip or shove and you’re on the canvas.
Hopping with both feet leaving the floor at once.
Letting the feet come together and narrowing the base.

drills.name: Lead-foot pivot
drills.desc: Spinning on the ball of the lead foot to swing the rear leg through an arc, changing the angle without giving ground. A sharp pivot takes you off the line of attack and puts your power hand where the opponent isn't facing. Throw it behind the jab or lead hook to exit combinations safely.
mistakes: Pivoting on a flat foot instead of the ball of the foot.
Standing tall out of stance during the turn.
Pivoting without a punch or feint to cover the movement.

drills.name: Cutting the ring
drills.desc: Herding a mobile opponent toward the ropes by stepping laterally to close escape angles instead of chasing in straight lines. The pressure fighter's craft: small diagonal steps, feints to freeze, and position taken one half-step at a time. Requires legs that stay fresh late in the fight.
mistakes: Following the opponent in a straight line instead of stepping to where they’re going.
Lunging with big steps and getting countered mid-stride.
Cutting the ring with the hands down as you close distance.

drills.name: Shadowboxing rounds
drills.desc: Timed rounds of imaginary sparring: moving, punching and defending against an opponent you visualise. It's where technique is rehearsed without impact — every session should have a theme, not random arm-waving. The mirror is the coach; watch the guard, the stance, the balance.
mistakes: Throwing arm punches with no footwork or head movement between them.
Working without a plan — pick one theme per round.
Never visualising return fire, so defense disappears.

drills.name: Double-end bag
drills.desc: A small ball strung between floor and ceiling that snaps back unpredictably after every punch. It punishes slow hands and lazy feet, forcing accurate straight punches, constant distance management, and head movement between shots. The closest a bag gets to a live opponent.
mistakes: Loading up on power shots — the bag rewards speed and accuracy, not force.
Standing flat-footed in one spot instead of moving with the rebound.
Watching your own gloves instead of the bag.

drills.name: Jump rope rounds
drills.desc: The boxer's classic conditioning tool: timed rounds of skipping that build springy calves, wrist speed and rhythm on the balls of the feet. Progress from basic bounce to boxer skip, crossovers and double-unders. Ten minutes of rope teaches the light feet that hours of running can't.
mistakes: Jumping too high — the rope needs only an inch of clearance.
Swinging from the shoulders instead of turning the wrists.
Landing on flat feet and pounding the heels.

drills.name: Heavy bag rounds
drills.desc: Timed rounds of continuous output on the bag. Builds punch endurance, breathing rhythm and the habit of staying busy while tired.
mistakes: Pushing the bag instead of snapping punches.
Holding breath — exhale on every shot.
